title: Arabic and Islamic Psychology and Philosophy of Mind

summaries.example: Imagine seeing a friend across a playground. Your eyes receive the sight, your inner senses put the details together, your memory recognizes the friend, and your thinking helps you decide whether to wave. The philosophers in this entry asked how all these parts work together.
summaries.summary: This entry explains how philosophers writing in the Arabic and Islamic tradition studied the soul and mind from about the ninth through twelfth centuries. Their “science of the soul” included more than reasoning: it covered the senses, imagination, memory, bodily organs, desire, and intellect. They drew heavily on Aristotle, while also using ideas influenced by Plato and Neoplatonic writers. Al-Kindi described parts of perception and several kinds of intellect, but his views do not form one complete system. Razi connected different kinds of soul with bodily organs while treating the rational soul as nonphysical and immortal. Al-Farabi described a potential intellect becoming active with help from a separate Agent Intellect, and he linked knowledge with human happiness. Avicenna argued strongly that the soul is an independent, self-aware, immortal substance. He also gave a detailed account of inner senses, including estimation and different kinds of imagination. Averroes stayed closer to Aristotle and criticized adding estimation as a separate sense, but he developed difficult theories about the material and Agent intellects. Across the entry, the thinkers seek to explain both ordinary mental activities and the hope of reaching universal truth.
key_ideas: Muslim philosophers studied the soul as part of a larger search for knowledge.
They connected the senses, imagination, memory, and intellect in different ways.
Al-Kindi and Razi offered early ideas; al-Farabi developed them; Avicenna and Averroes gave different, detailed accounts.
Many of these thinkers joined ideas from Aristotle with ideas influenced by Plato and later Greek writers.
They disagreed about whether the soul is closely tied to the body, how knowledge begins, and how the intellect reaches truth.
summaries.why_it_matters: These ideas show that questions about the mind have a long and varied history. They also show how philosophers can combine, revise, and criticize earlier traditions. Studying their explanations helps us ask careful questions about memory, imagination, knowledge, the body, and the possibility of lasting truth.

important_terms.definition: The soul, or nafs, means the life-principle studied by these philosophers. It includes abilities such as sensing, imagining, remembering, and thinking.
The intellect is the ability connected with understanding ideas, especially general ideas that are not tied to only one object.
The imagination is the ability to keep, change, and bring back pictures or other mental images.
The Agent Intellect is a higher, separate source that philosophers such as al-Farabi and Avicenna said helps human beings understand ideas.

questions_to_think_about: When you recognize something, what roles might seeing and remembering play?
Can a person think about a general idea, such as fairness, from particular experiences?
Why might philosophers disagree about whether the soul can exist without the body?

summaries.example: Suppose you see a wolf. The external senses receive its visible form, while internal powers preserve and interpret what is sensed. Avicenna explains the animal’s fearful response through estimation, which detects a non-sensible significance in the perceived object. Averroes instead gives imagination and memory more of this work, resisting estimation as an additional internal sense. The example illustrates that the disagreement concerns not merely terminology but the architecture of cognition.
summaries.summary: The entry traces a major strand of classical Arabic and Islamic philosophy of mind from al-Kindi and Razi through al-Farabi, Avicenna, and Averroes. “Psychology” here is not restricted to modern theories of consciousness: it includes physiology, external and internal senses, imagination, memory, desire, practical reasoning, theoretical intellect, and the soul’s possible perfection. Aristotle supplies the dominant framework, especially through On the Soul and related works, but Hellenistic commentaries and Neoplatonic interpretations reshape it. Al-Kindi combines accounts of perception, universals, and four intellects, though his surviving positions remain fragmentary and sometimes pull in different directions. Razi gives the soul a Platonic structure and assigns bodily locations to subordinate faculties while treating rational soul as nonphysical and immortal. Al-Farabi develops a hierarchy in which sensible forms reach imagination and prepare the potential intellect, while the separate Agent Intellect actualizes intelligible understanding. Intellectual development approaches, but does not simply become identical with, that higher intellect. Avicenna offers the most explicit defense of an independent, self-conscious soul. His thought experiment of a person suspended without sensory contact is meant to show that self-awareness is not reducible to bodily perception. His detailed inner psychology includes common sense, formative and compositive imagination, estimation, cogitation, memory, and recollection. He later works to protect rational intellect from being absorbed into these bodily faculties. key_ideas: Classical Muslim philosophers treated psychology as a broad inquiry into the soul, combining physiological description with questions about knowledge and ultimate perfection.
Their Aristotelian inheritance was modified by Platonic and Neoplatonic themes, especially concerning the soul’s immateriality, ascent, and relation to universal truth.
Al-Kindi presents several intellects and an extramission account of vision in some works, but the evidence does not yield a fully integrated psychology.
Al-Farabi makes the Agent Intellect central to the transition from potential to actual understanding and connects intellectual perfection with happiness.
Avicenna defends an independently existing, self-aware, immortal soul and develops a complex account of internal senses, including estimation and cogitation.
Averroes moves closer to Aristotle, rejects estimation as a separate internal sense, and offers changing accounts of the material intellect and its relation to the Agent Intellect.
summaries.why_it_matters: The entry matters because it reveals psychology as a meeting point of natural science, epistemology, metaphysics, and religiously meaningful questions about perfection and immortality. It also demonstrates that “the Islamic philosophical tradition” was not a single view: its major figures inherited overlapping sources but proposed substantially different models of cognition, embodiment, individuality, and intellectual fulfillment.

important_terms.definition: The soul, or nafs, is the life-principle and the subject of psychological abilities, including nutrition, sensation, imagination, memory, and intellect.
A potential intellect is a capacity prepared to receive intelligible forms; it becomes actual when it is actively thinking those forms.
The Agent Intellect is a separate, immaterial principle said to actualize the human intellect and make intelligible forms available.
An intelligible is a universal or abstract object of understanding rather than a particular material thing as sensed.
Estimation, or wahm, is Avicenna’s proposed faculty for grasping non-sensible intentions, such as an animal’s immediate sense of danger.
The hylomorphic view explains a thing through matter and form. Averroes applies related ideas to the hierarchy and development of the soul.
Conjunction is the proposed union or close relation between a perfected human intellect and the Agent Intellect.

questions_to_think_about: Does explaining thought through bodily organs undermine the claim that intellect is immaterial, or could the two explanations serve different purposes?
What is gained, and what is lost, when Avicenna adds estimation as an internal sense?
Why might a philosopher identify human happiness with intellectual perfection rather than with pleasure or ordinary success?
Does Averroes’s account preserve individual thinking if the material intellect is separate from individual bodies?
How do the thinkers use the idea of the Agent Intellect to explain both ordinary learning and exceptional knowledge such as prophecy?

summaries.example: Think about studying a new idea. First, you see words or diagrams. Your senses receive them, imagination helps hold their images, and memory lets you recall them later. Al-Farabi says the potential intellect needs help from the Agent Intellect to understand the idea as a general concept. Avicenna gives inner powers such as estimation and cogitation more detailed jobs. Averroes keeps the system simpler and says imagination and memory can do much of that work.
summaries.summary: This entry explores how several major philosophers in the Arabic and Islamic tradition explained the soul and its powers. From roughly the ninth to twelfth centuries, they studied sensation, imagination, memory, desire, bodily organs, reasoning, and the intellect. Their work was strongly influenced by Aristotle, especially his writings on the soul and senses, but it also included Platonic and Neoplatonic ideas. Al-Kindi described perception as moving from objects through the senses and inner powers, and he proposed several kinds of intellect. His surviving views are important but do not form one perfectly unified theory. Razi described three kinds of soul and connected the lower ones with organs such as the liver and heart, while treating rational soul as nonphysical and immortal. Al-Farabi organized the process of understanding around a potential human intellect and a separate Agent Intellect. The Agent Intellect helps turn a capacity for thought into actual understanding. Al-Farabi also connected intellectual growth with happiness and with the highest human perfection. Avicenna gave the soul a particularly independent role. He argued that a person can be aware of the self even without sensory experience, and he described the soul as self-conscious and immortal. He divided inner mental activities into several powers, including common sense, imagination, estimation, cogitation, memory, and recollection. Averroes criticized some of these divisions. He thought imagination and memory could explain work that Avicenna assigned to estimation. He also developed complex accounts of the material intellect and Agent Intellect, sometimes treating them as separate immaterial principles. key_ideas: These philosophers studied the whole soul, not just the part we call the mind today.
They used Aristotle’s writings but changed them through Platonic and Neoplatonic ideas.
Al-Kindi and Razi began important discussions about vision, memory, the soul, and different kinds of intellect.
Al-Farabi described learning as the potential intellect becoming active with help from the Agent Intellect.
Avicenna argued that the soul is self-aware and can exist independently of the body, while giving a detailed account of inner senses.
Averroes followed Aristotle more closely and disagreed with Avicenna about the number and jobs of inner senses and about the material intellect.
summaries.why_it_matters: The ideas in this entry matter because they ask questions that still sound familiar: How do we recognize things? How does memory support thinking? Is the mind just a bodily process? Can knowledge change who we are? Comparing these philosophers teaches us that careful disagreement can produce different models of the same human experiences.

important_terms.definition: The soul is the life-principle studied by these philosophers. It includes bodily and mental abilities, from nutrition and sensation to imagination and reasoning.
The intellect is the power of understanding, especially general ideas and truths rather than only individual things.
A potential intellect is a capacity for understanding that has not yet become active in thought.
The Agent Intellect is a separate higher intellect that helps make ideas understandable and helps human intellects become active.
An internal sense is a mental ability that works with information after the external senses receive it, such as imagination, memory, or estimation.
Estimation is Avicenna’s name for a power that notices an object’s meaningful but non-sensible features, such as danger.
Conjunction means the intellect’s reaching a close union with the Agent Intellect in the highest form of understanding.

questions_to_think_about: Is remembering a picture the same as understanding a general idea? Why or why not?
Why might two philosophers explain the same fearful reaction using different mental powers?
If knowledge makes someone more like a perfect intellect, would gaining knowledge also make that person happier?
What might be a strength of Avicenna’s detailed model? What might be a strength of Averroes’s simpler one?
